question: Why is water called the universal solvent?

passages.title: Why Is Water Called the Universal Solvent?
passages.text: You may hear water called the universal solvent. Here is a look at whether this is true and why water is so good at dissolving other compounds. Polarity Makes Water a Great Solvent Water dissolves more compounds than any other solvent. The biggest reason water is a great solvent is because it’s a polar molecule. What this means is that water is a neutral atom, but one part has a partial positive charge and another part has a partial negative charge. A water molecule has a bent shape with a 104.5 degree angle between the two hydrogen atoms, causing the polarity. The two hydrogen atoms of each water molecule have a partial positive charge, while the oxygen atom has a partial negative charge. Polar molecules readily dissolve in water because the positive part of the polar molecule is attracted to the oxygen atom, while the negative part is attracted to the hydrogen atom. In addition to polarity, water is a great solvent because it is amphoteric. What this means is that water can act as both an acid and a base. passages.title: Why Is Water Called the Universal Solvent? - Biology Insights
passages.text: Water is often called the “universal solvent” because it can dissolve a wider range of substances than any other liquid on Earth. Its pervasive presence and solvent properties are fundamental to many processes, from supporting life within biological systems to shaping geological landscapes. Understanding why water possesses such remarkable dissolving capabilities is key to appreciating its widespread influence. Water’s Unique Molecular Structure Water’s remarkable solvent properties stem from its distinctive molecular structure. A water molecule (H₂O) consists of one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms, forming a bent shape. Oxygen’s higher electronegativity results in an unequal distribution of electrical charge. The oxygen atom acquires a slight negative charge, while the hydrogen atoms develop slight positive charges, making water a polar molecule. This polarity allows water molecules to form hydrogen bonds, which are weak attractions between the slightly positive hydrogen of one water molecule and the slightly negative oxygen of another. These hydrogen bonds allow water molecules to interact extensively with each other and with other charged or polar substances. This ability to engage in strong intermolecular attractions is foundational to its role as an effective solvent. More kinetic energy results in more interaction between particles, so dissolving occurs more quickly. Why Water Isn’t Really a Universal Solvent Water dissolves polar molecules, including salts, sugars, many gases, proteins, simple alcohols, and DNA. But, it isn’t a universal solvent because it can’t dissolve hydrophobic or nonpolar molecules, such as fats, oils, some hydroxides, and most metal oxides, silicates, and sulfides. There is no true universal solvent. The alchemists sought such a compound, which they called alkahest. One problem with a universal solvent would be its ability to dissolve any container. The alchemists got around this issue by stating alkahest could only dissolve compounds and not elements. Of course, such a substance does not exist, but the alchemists did find useful solvents, such as caustic potash in alcohol. References - Ball, Philip (2001). Example: Dissolving Salt in Water For example, consider how ordinary table salt (NaCl) dissolves in water. Salt is an ionic compound that dissolves into a sodium ion (Na+) and a chlorine ion (Cl–). When you stir salt into water, the water molecules orient so that the negatively-charged oxygen atoms face the positively-charged sodium atoms in salt, while the positively-charged hydrogen atoms face the negatively-charged chlorine atoms. The ionic bond is a strong chemical bond, but the action of all the water molecules is sufficient to pull the sodium and chlorine atoms apart. Once separated, the ions evenly distribute and form a chemical solution. This brings up an important point about solvents. Their activity depends on temperature. If you add salt to ice water, very little dissolves. If you add salt to boiling water, much more salt dissolves. Raising the temperature typically increases the effectiveness of a solvent because it increases the kinetic energy of particles. Substances Water Does Not Dissolve Water does not dissolve nonpolar substances like oils, fats, and waxes. Nonpolar molecules lack the uneven distribution of electrical charge found in water. Without these partial charges, water molecules cannot form strong electrostatic attractions with nonpolar solutes. This difference in molecular structure prevents water from effectively interacting with nonpolar molecules. Nonpolar substances do not dissolve in water due to the “hydrophobic effect,” meaning “water-fearing.” Water molecules prefer to form hydrogen bonds with each other. When nonpolar molecules are present, they disrupt this hydrogen-bonding network. Water molecules push nonpolar substances together to minimize disruption and maximize their own hydrogen bonding, causing them to separate, as seen with oil and water. Real-World Significance Water’s role as a universal solvent is significant across biological, geological, and everyday contexts. In living organisms, water facilitates the transport of nutrients, minerals, and gases throughout the body. It also serves as the medium for biochemical reactions within cells. Water’s ability to dissolve waste products allows for their efficient removal from the body. Geologically, water’s solvent power contributes to weathering and erosion, shaping the Earth’s surface.

Substances Water Dissolves Water’s polarity enables it to dissolve a broad spectrum of substances, including ionic and polar covalent compounds. When ionic compounds, like table salt, are introduced to water, water molecules surround and separate the individual ions. The slightly negative oxygen ends of water molecules are attracted to positively charged ions, while the slightly positive hydrogen ends are drawn to negatively charged ions. This process, known as solvation, weakens the forces holding the ionic compound together, causing it to dissociate and disperse uniformly. Water also dissolves polar covalent compounds, such as sugar or alcohol. These compounds possess uneven charge distributions, creating partial positive and negative regions. Water molecules form hydrogen bonds and other electrostatic interactions with these polar regions, pulling the solute molecules into solution. This interaction overcomes the intermolecular forces within the solute, allowing the polar covalent compound to dissolve as whole molecules rather than dissociating into ions.
